meters.label: Servers running v2 and serving users

frames.narration: Six servers run v1 and share 500 requests per second. Each handles 100, so 5 is the minimum. We will ship v2 as a rolling update with max surge 1 and max unavailable 0.
Surge first: a seventh server starts, running v2. It is not in the load balancer yet. Its readiness check fails while it boots and warms up, so no user reaches it.
The readiness check passes, so the load balancer adds the v2 server. Now both versions serve live traffic from the same database. This mixed-version period lasts until the last v1 server is gone.

Only now is one v1 server removed, and with connection draining. The load balancer stops sending it new requests, waits for in-flight ones to finish, then stops it. No user sees an error, and 6 servers stay ready.
The cycle repeats: start one v2, wait for ready, drain one v1. Capacity never falls below 6 servers, so 500 req/s is always served. Halfway through, 3 servers run v1 and 3 run v2.

After six cycles all servers run v2 and the rollout ends. If v2 had a bug, the way back would be another rolling update in reverse, taking as long as this one, with the bad version still serving meanwhile.

Now the alternative, blue-green, starting again from 6 x v1: build a full green set of 6 x v2 beside blue. Blue keeps all the traffic. Cost doubles to 12 servers while both exist, and green can be tested for real.
Every green server is ready, so the router flips once. All 500 req/s go to green at the same moment. Users see v1 or v2, never a mix, and blue stays up, idle, as the rollback target.

If green misbehaves, flipping the router back restores v1 in about a second. If it stays healthy, blue is shut down after a soak period, and only then is the old column dropped from the database (contract).
